chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Abdillah ibn al-Mughira from Jamil from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah honored the believers with Friday, so the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) established it as good news for them and as a rebuke to the hypocrites. Therefore, it is not proper to leave them; whoever leaves them intentionally has no prayer.

His saying (peace be upon him) 'no prayer for him' is understood in two ways: one is that if he leaves reading these two Surahs not believing that there is much merit and abundant reward in their recitation, then he has no prayer; and it is also possible that he meant (peace be upon him) 'no complete, superior prayer for him,' as the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'No prayer for the neighbor of the mosque except in his mosque.' And he meant (peace be upon him and his family) no superior, complete prayer, without the meaning being the invalidation of its validity, and similarly is the report that he narrated.

key_terms.السُّورَتَيْنِ: The two Surahs (referring to Qaf and Al-Dhariyat)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on intentionally leaving the Friday Surah recitations?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), highlighting Friday as a divine honor for believers and a rebuke for hypocrites. The phrase 'no prayer for him' is interpreted by scholars as indicating a lack of excellence (*fadhilah*) rather than total invalidation, contingent upon whether the omission stems from disbelief in the merit or mere negligence. This underscores the spiritual significance of Friday rituals in Shia jurisprudence as acts of devotion that enhance the quality of worship.
